text: The Script Debugger only ever attaches to ServiceNow's server-side engine. Client Scripts don't run there at all — they run as real JavaScript in the user's actual browser, the same runtime as any other website. The right tool is the browser's own DevTools: Chrome, Firefox, or Edge all ship one.

DevTools' Sources tab lists every JavaScript file the page has loaded, and a fired Client Script is one of those files. Clicking a line number there sets a real breakpoint. In this onChange script, breaking on the line reading the category field pauses the browser the instant you change Priority on the actual form, showing the call stack and every variable in scope.

Not every question needs a full breakpoint. Dropping console.log calls directly into the script — logging the old and new priority, then the current category — is the fastest way to confirm a value without pausing anything. Every output lands in the Console tab, in order, as the script actually runs.

The Console isn't limited to reading printed output — you can type JavaScript directly into it, against the live page. Typing g_form into the Console on any open form returns the live GlideForm object, so you can call g_form.getValue of priority by hand. Typing g_user does the same for the current session, like checking g_user.hasRole of admin, with no script line added at all.

None of this is ServiceNow-specific tooling. It's standard front-end web development practice — breakpoints, console logging, and live evaluation — applied to the simple fact that Client Scripts are real JavaScript running in a real browser, just like any other site a front-end developer debugs.

Breakpoints in Sources, console.log for a quick trace, and live evaluation of g_form and g_user in the Console — three tools, the same three moves every time. Next lesson is the Debugging Lab: a real bug in a Script Include, traced with gs.info and fixed.
